> Fix #110996

Isn't this documented and expected behavior? 
From https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/httpclient-factory-troubleshooting#different-typed-clients-are-registered-on-a-common-interface

> DO NOT register multiple typed clients on a single interface without explicitly specifying the name.

Also doesn't it just create the inverse problem? Ie. you'd not be able to reuse a single concrete type for multiple interfaces (though I don't know if that's a valid use case to begin with)

> > Fix #110996
> 
> Isn't this documented and expected behavior? From https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/httpclient-factory-troubleshooting#different-typed-clients-are-registered-on-a-common-interface
> 
> > DO NOT register multiple typed clients on a single interface without explicitly specifying the name.
> 
> Also doesn't it just create the inverse problem? Ie. you'd not be able to reuse a single concrete type for multiple interfaces (though I don't know if that's a valid use case to begin with)

It's so common to have one interface with multiple implementation and it is also common to add one interface with multiple implementations; actually it is the whole definition of IoC. Meanwhile it's not common to add one implementation with two interface.
Also if you think that's a serious problem, I can simply concat the name of the interface with the name of the implementation so it would fix both problems

> #110996 is not a bug, and the proposed change is breaking. Please refer to [#110996 (comment)](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/110996#issuecomment-2594126840) for further explanations.
> 
> @stormaref Re: why this change is breaking:
> 
> 1. Consider, e.g. the code that depended on the name being the specific value (like, a configuration section key)
> 
> ```cs
> // load all named clients from configuration
> foreach (var section in configuration.GetSection("HttpClientSettings").GetChildren())
> {
>     serviceCollection.AddHttpClient(section.Key)
>         .UseSocketsHttpHandler(b => b.Configure(section));
> }
> 
> // additional setup for a typed client
> serviceCollection.AddHttpClient<ITypedClient, Foo>()
>     .UseSocketsHttpHandler((shh, _) =>
>     {
>         shh.SslOptions = ....
>     });
> ```
> 
>  ```
> {
>   "HttpClientSettings": {
>     "ITypedClient": {
>       "UseCookies": false,
>       "ConnectTimeout": "00:00:05"
>     },
>     ....
>   }
> }
> ```
> 
> In case above, the typed client's underlying named client "ITypedClient" would get configured from the respective section alongside the programmatic configuration. But the proposed change would lead to loosing the config from the configuration section (as the name will change). That might lead to e.g. unexpected hangs, as ConnectTimeout in infinity by default.
> 
> 2. This can also be the other way around, a code that depended on the name NOT being the specific value
> 
> ```cs
> serviceCollection.AddHttpClient<ITypedClient, Foo>(
>     c => c.BaseAddress = new Uri("https://example.com/")));
> 
> serviceCollection.AddHttpClient("Foo",
>     c => c.BaseAddress = new Uri("https://api.github.com/")); // unrelated to ITypedClient!
> ```
> 
> In case above, there were two separate named clients "ITypedClient" and "Foo", but after the proposed change, only one client "Foo" will remain, so all the settings will be unexpectedly merged/overwritten.
> 
> These are two random examples that would break from simply updating the package.

The way that I implemented it was an idea, we can simply concat the name of the interface with the name of the implementation and fix the issues you said.

> we can simply concat the name of the interface with the name of the implementation and fix the issues you said.

Whatever you'd put there -- be it implementation name, or concatenation, or any other kind of transformation, random generation even -- case (1) is _100% broken_ since it's simply _not_ the name that was there before.

And case (2) would always have a _non-zero_ chance to be broken. Whichever string you'll choose, there's a possibility there was another client with such a name.

Thank you for your suggestion, but I want to clarify that I’m not looking for a workaround for this issue. My goal is to address and fix it for good. While there are alternative ways to handle this scenario, the current behavior is counterintuitive and inconsistent with the expected functionality of dependency injection. This is something that should work out of the box without requiring extra workarounds.
Hi @stormaref sorry for the delay. I am now back from winter vacation and will get back to you shortly.

> This issue has been present since at least .NET 7 and continues to occur in .NET 8 and .NET 9. The behavior where multiple `HttpClient` instances with the same interface overwrite each other's configurations has persisted across these versions.

You are making this seem like it is some sort of bug @stormaref but it is pretty clear to me that using the interface as the option name for `HttpClient` configuration was intentional and thus everything is working by design.

I'm not necessarily saying I don't _like_ the proposal, but I see it as a feature and not a bug.

Now, as for the issue itself, I'd rather the .NET team came up with a more general approach to link dependent services together instead of this hacky approach they keep applying every single time a new coupling is needed (started with `Logger<T>`, then `Options<T>`, then `HttpClient`, then `Metrics`...). Instead of creating these specialized extensions each with a completely custom implementation behind the scenes, the container API should allow you to more seamlessly defined dependent services using a reusable API that can be used for all existing cases, and all future dependency cases.

Why do you think it is not a bug?

> Why do you think it is not a bug?

Because registrations are based on the service interface, not on the concrete type. That's how `AddHttpClient` was designed. It takes the name of the interface to name an underlying `Options<T>` object that stores information about the specific `HttpMessageHandler` which is the thing that varies and has a custom lifetime.

It was not meant to be used like you did there.

> > Why do you think it is not a bug?
> 
> Because registrations are based on the service interface, not on the concrete type. That's how `AddHttpClient` was designed. It takes the name of the interface to name an underlying `Options<T>` object that stores information about the specific `HttpMessageHandler` which is the thing that varies and has a custom lifetime.

Why do we use interfaces for registering our services? It goes without saying that it is because of inversion of control. Given this, it would be a bug

I believe this introduces a breaking change. However, if you're looking to have multiple implementations for an interface, you can take advantage of the options available for named and typed HttpClients. It’s a great way to handle different scenarios!

There are indeed several ways to achieve this, but this is something that ought to work as expected out of the box. With dependency injection, the expected behavior is to allow different implementations of an interface to coexist without conflicts. However, the current setup leads to issues, as evidenced by many people encountering this problem.

Here’s a related discussion on StackOverflow that highlights this issue: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/74005464/add-httpclients-with-same-interface-ended-up-having-the-same-base-url-asp-net-co

Also, what is the problem with changing this behavior? What do you think could go wrong with allowing multiple HttpClient registrations under the same interface to retain their independent configurations?
